title: C#, the deeper parts
blurb: Async internals, LINQ semantics, generics variance, records and the memory types: the C# questions after 'what's a value type'.

questions.q: In ASP.NET Core application code (not a library), what does adding `ConfigureAwait(false)` to an await change?
choices: Very little: there is no SynchronizationContext, so continuations already resume on the thread pool
It moves the awaited call onto a background thread so the request thread stays free for other work
It prevents the deadlock that calling `.Result` in a controller action would otherwise cause
It stops the ExecutionContext flowing, so AsyncLocal values and the current culture are lost
questions.why: ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so there is nothing to capture and nothing to skip. Libraries still use `ConfigureAwait(false)` because they may be called from WPF, WinForms or legacy ASP.NET, where it avoids a context hop. It never moves work to another thread, and ExecutionContext (AsyncLocal) flows either way.
questions.asked: Filters cargo-cult answers; a strong candidate says why libraries still use it and app code can drop it.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?
choices: Nothing: awaiting a completed ValueTask again returns the stored result, exactly as Task does
It does not compile: a ValueTask<T> must be awaited inline and cannot be stored in a local variable
The second await blocks forever, because a ValueTask signals its completion to one awaiter only
A ValueTask may be awaited only once; it can wrap a pooled source that is reused after the first await
questions.why: A ValueTask can be backed by a pooled IValueTaskSource that is recycled once consumed, so a second await (or awaiting it concurrently, or calling `.Result` before completion) is undefined behaviour. It may happen to work in a test. If you need to await twice, call `.AsTask()` once and keep the Task. Storing it in a local is legal; the rule is about consuming it.
questions.asked: A "have you read the ValueTask guidance" question; the follow-up is when ValueTask is worth it at all (hot paths that usually complete synchronously).

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: b
a
One or more errors occurred. (a) (b)
a and then b, on two separate lines
questions.why: Both tasks fault, and the task from `WhenAll` holds an AggregateException with both. `await` unwraps it and rethrows only the first inner exception, in argument order, so you see "a". The AggregateException message is what `.Wait()` or `.Result` would surface. To log every failure, keep the WhenAll task and read `task.Exception.InnerExceptions` in the catch.
questions.asked: Catches people who log the caught exception and believe they have seen every failure in a batch.

questions.q: What does `await foreach` give you here that returning `Task<List<int>>` would not?
choices: The three delays run in parallel, so the whole loop completes in about 100 ms instead of 300
Each number is handled on its own thread-pool thread, so the loop bodies run concurrently
Each number is printed as soon as it is produced, about 100 ms apart, not all at the end
Nothing at runtime: the compiler buffers the sequence into a List before the loop starts
questions.why: An async iterator streams: the consumer gets each item as soon as the producer yields it, and the producer awaits between items without blocking a thread. The loop is still sequential, one item at a time, so nothing runs in parallel. That makes it a good fit for paging through an API or streaming rows from a database without loading everything into memory first.
questions.asked: Asked when the job involves streaming or paging; a strong answer names a real use such as EF Core `AsAsyncEnumerable()`.

questions.q: What does the semaphore achieve here?
choices: Requests run in batches of four, and each batch waits for the slowest request of the previous batch
Only four threads are used, and the remaining requests queue on the thread pool until one is free
The first four URLs are fetched, and later calls are skipped once the semaphore count reaches zero
At most four requests are in flight at once, and the others wait asynchronously without blocking
questions.why: The semaphore is a sliding window: whenever one request finishes and releases, the next waiting one starts, so there are no batches. `WaitAsync` waits without holding a thread, which is the whole point versus `Wait()`. It is the standard way to be polite to a downstream API. `Parallel.ForEachAsync` with `MaxDegreeOfParallelism` does the same job.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can control concurrency, not only start it; the follow-up is "what if one URL hangs?" (timeouts, cancellation).

questions.q: What is the most serious bug in this minimal API endpoint?
choices: The discard `_ =` tells the compiler to drop the call, so the confirmation is never sent at all
Task.Run blocks the request thread until SendConfirmationAsync completes, removing any benefit
The background work uses the request-scoped DbContext, which is disposed when the request ends
Results.Accepted() needs a location URI for the new order, so the endpoint returns a 500 error
questions.why: The DbContext is scoped to the request, so the fire-and-forget task races its disposal and fails with ObjectDisposedException, or worse, shares a non-thread-safe context. Its exceptions are also unobserved and the work is lost on shutdown. The discard only silences the "not awaited" warning. The fix is a queue drained by a BackgroundService that creates its own scope.
questions.asked: Real production bug; a strong answer names both the lifetime problem and the lost-on-restart problem.

questions.q: In .NET 9, in what order does this print the results?
choices: In the order of `ids`, because WhenEach keeps the input order exactly as Task.WhenAll does
All at once, after the slowest task finishes, because WhenEach waits for every task first
In completion order, but faulted tasks are skipped so the loop only sees successful ones
In completion order: each task is yielded as soon as it finishes, whether it succeeded or not
questions.why: `Task.WhenEach` (new in .NET 9) returns an IAsyncEnumerable of the tasks in the order they complete. It hands you the task itself, so a faulted one is yielded like any other and `await t` rethrows its exception. Before .NET 9 the same pattern was a `Task.WhenAny` loop, which is O(n²) and easy to get wrong.
questions.asked: A currency check on recent .NET; the follow-up is what people wrote before it existed.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: It throws: a LINQ query can be enumerated only once
questions.why: `squares` is a query, not a result. `Sum` and `Max` each enumerate it, so the selector runs once per element on each call, six in total. Against a database or an expensive projection that means doing the work twice, which is what analysers flag as "possible multiple enumeration". Materialise once with `ToList()` when you need the results more than once.
questions.asked: Checks that you understand deferred execution well enough to spot its cost, not only recite its definition.

questions.q: You look up a user by email. Emails must be unique, and a missing user is a normal outcome. Which call fits?
choices: `FirstOrDefault`: it returns null when nothing matches and throws when two users match
`Single`: it returns null when nothing matches and throws when two users match
`SingleOrDefault`: it returns null when nothing matches and throws when two users match
`First`: it returns the default value when nothing matches and ignores any duplicates
questions.why: `SingleOrDefault` encodes both rules: none is fine, more than one is a data bug you want to hear about. `FirstOrDefault` never complains about duplicates, and `Single` and `First` throw when nothing matches. In EF Core, `Single*` asks the database for two rows so it can detect the duplicate, which costs almost nothing.
questions.asked: Simple, but the reasoning shows whether you let the API encode your invariants.

questions.q: On a plain `IEnumerable<T>` returned by a LINQ query, why prefer `Any()` to `Count() > 0`?
choices: `Count()` copies the sequence into a List first, so it allocates on every call
`Any()` caches its answer after the first call, while `Count()` re-runs each time
`Any()` stops at the first element, while `Count()` has to walk the whole sequence
`Count() > 0` throws on an empty sequence, while `Any()` simply returns false
questions.why: Existence needs one element, and counting needs all of them. For a filtered sequence of a million items that is the difference between one step and a million. For an `ICollection<T>` such as a List, `Count()` reads the stored count, so both are cheap there. Nothing is cached and nothing is copied.
questions.asked: A quick signal of whether you think about what your LINQ calls actually do.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: The lambda captures the variable `min`, not its value at the time `Where` was called. The query runs when `Count()` enumerates it, by which point `min` is 20, so only 25 passes. The same capture causes bugs when a query is built in a loop and the loop variable changes before enumeration. Materialise the query, or copy the value into a local, to pin it.
questions.asked: Combines closures with deferred execution; a strong answer mentions the loop-variable variant.

questions.q: Against EF Core, what SQL does this run?
choices: A SELECT with WHERE Total > 1000, because EF Core decompiles the delegate into SQL
A SELECT of every order with no WHERE clause; the filter then runs in memory
None: EF Core 3+ throws because the predicate would have to be evaluated on the client
A SELECT with WHERE Total > 1000, because Where on an IQueryable always becomes SQL
questions.why: `Queryable.Where` takes an `Expression<Func<T, bool>>`, which EF can translate. A `Func` variable cannot convert to an expression tree, so overload resolution picks `Enumerable.Where`, and the query is enumerated as a plain IEnumerable: the whole table streams into memory. There is no exception, because EF never sees the predicate. Declare it as `Expression<Func<Order, bool>>` instead.
questions.asked: Shows up when someone "refactors a predicate into a variable" and the page gets slow; it separates people who know how LINQ providers work.

questions.q: Which of these lines compile?
choices: Line A only: `IEnumerable<out T>` is covariant, while `List<T>` is invariant
Both: string converts to object, so any generic of string converts as well
Line B only: `List<T>` implements `IEnumerable<T>`, so it inherits covariance
Neither: a generic type never converts between different type arguments
questions.why: `IEnumerable<T>` is declared `out T` because it only hands values out, so a sequence of strings is safely a sequence of objects. `List<T>` also accepts values in (`Add`), and allowing line B would let you add an int to a list of strings, so classes are always invariant. Only interfaces and delegates can declare variance.
questions.asked: Variance comes up when designing repository or handler interfaces; knowing why List is invariant is the real test.

questions.q: What does the `notnull` constraint give you on `class Cache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull`?
choices: A runtime ArgumentNullException whenever a caller passes a null key
A compile error for every reference-type key, since references can be null
A nullable warning when someone uses `string?` or `int?` as the key type
It restricts TKey to value types only, exactly like `where TKey : struct`
questions.why: `notnull` is part of nullable reference types: it allows both value and reference types but warns when a nullable type argument is used. Like the rest of NRT it is a compile-time check with no runtime effect. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` declares its key the same way, because a null key has no hash code.
questions.asked: Tells the interviewer whether you have written generic library code under nullable reference types.

questions.q: What do static abstract interface members (C# 11) make possible?
choices: Calling a static method directly on the interface, without naming any implementing type
Generic code that calls a static method or operator on T, such as `T.Parse` or `a + b`
Overriding a base class static method and dispatching to it at runtime through a base reference
Giving every implementing class one shared static field that the interface itself owns
questions.why: A constraint such as `where T : INumber<T>` lets a generic method write `T.Zero` or `a + b`, resolved per type argument at compile time. That is what generic math and `IParsable<T>` are built on. You still cannot call an abstract static on the interface itself, and there is no runtime dispatch through a base reference.
questions.asked: Awareness question; a good answer mentions `IParsable<T>` or generic math rather than inventing a use.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: False
True
True for `==`, but False for `a.Equals(b)`
It does not compile: records need an explicit `==`
questions.why: Record equality compares each member with its own `Equals`. For `List<string>` that is reference equality, and the two lists are different objects, so the records are not equal even though the contents match. `==` and `Equals` always agree on records. Use an immutable collection with value semantics, or override `Equals`, if a collection must take part.
questions.asked: The classic record gotcha; it shows you know "value equality" is only as deep as each member.

questions.q: What does `public record Point(int X, int Y);` generate?
choices: Public mutable fields X and Y, a constructor, and reference equality inherited from object
Private fields X and Y, a constructor, and an Equals method that you must implement
Settable properties X and Y, a parameterless constructor, and value-based equality
Init-only properties X and Y, a constructor, Deconstruct, and value-based equality
questions.why: Positional parameters on a `record` (class) become public `init` properties, plus a primary constructor, `Deconstruct`, value equality, `ToString` and `with` support. On a `record struct` the properties are settable unless you write `readonly record struct`, which is the usual surprise.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know what the one-liner saves you from writing, and the record struct difference.

questions.q: What happens with this code (C# 11 or later)?
choices: It compiles; Email is null and the first read of it throws a NullReferenceException
It compiles with only a nullable warning, because `required` is advisory
It throws an ArgumentException at runtime from the generated constructor
Compile error: Email is required but the object initialiser does not set it
questions.why: `required` is enforced by the compiler at every construction site: an initialiser that omits the member is error CS9035, not a warning. `init` then stops it being reassigned after construction. System.Text.Json (.NET 7+) also honours `required` and rejects a payload without the property, which makes it useful on request DTOs.
questions.asked: Shows whether you use the modern alternatives to constructor-only DTOs.

questions.q: What does this print (C# 12)?
questions.why: A primary constructor parameter used inside a member is captured as a hidden mutable field. `Start` copied the value 5 once at construction, while `Next` keeps incrementing the captured parameter: 6, 7, then 8. The compiler warns (CS9124) that the parameter is stored twice. Primary constructor parameters are not properties and are not readonly.
questions.asked: Checks whether you have really used C# 12 primary constructors on classes, where they behave differently from records.

questions.q: What does the slice on the second line cost?
choices: One new 10-character string on the heap, the same cost as Substring
Nothing, because the compiler turns AsSpan into a string literal at build time
A new char array of 10 elements, copied from the string on the stack
Nothing new on the heap: it is a view over the original string memory
questions.why: A span is a pointer plus a length over memory that already exists, so slicing allocates nothing. That is why parsers use spans to avoid a Substring per field. The price is the ref struct rules: a span cannot live on the heap, so it cannot be a class field, be boxed, or be held across an await. Use `Memory<T>` when you need that.
questions.asked: Spans are the entry point to allocation-conscious .NET; the follow-up is why you cannot store one in a field.

questions.q: Why can a `Span<T>` not be stored in a field of a class?
choices: It is a ref struct that may point at stack memory, so it must never live on the heap
It is a class, and holding one in a field would keep the whole source array alive
It is immutable, and fields must be assignable after the constructor has run
It would be boxed on assignment, and boxing a span copies all of its elements
questions.why: A span can point at a `stackalloc` buffer. A heap object that outlived the stack frame would then point at freed memory, so the compiler forbids spans anywhere that could reach the heap: class fields, boxing, lambdas that capture them, and locals that cross an await. `Memory<T>` is the heap-safe counterpart that you convert to a span when you use it.
questions.asked: Tests understanding of why the restrictions exist, not only that they do.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: It does not compile: you cannot call a method on a readonly field
It throws at runtime because the readonly field is modified
questions.why: Calling a method on a `readonly` struct field makes the compiler pass a defensive copy, since it cannot prove `Inc` will not mutate the field. The copy is incremented and thrown away. Declaring the struct `readonly struct` (or the method `readonly`) removes the copies and makes the mutation a compile error instead of a silent no-op.
questions.asked: A deep one that separates people who have profiled struct-heavy code from those who have only read about value types.

questions.q: In .NET 9, what changes when the field you `lock` on is a `System.Threading.Lock` instead of an `object`?
choices: The lock becomes async-aware, so you can now `await` inside the lock block
The lock compiles to `Lock.EnterScope()`, a dedicated and faster primitive than Monitor
The lock is released automatically when the thread awaits inside the lock block
The lock is shared by every process on the machine, like a named system mutex
questions.why: C# 13 recognises the new `Lock` type and emits `EnterScope()` with a `using`, avoiding Monitor and the object header. Behaviour is otherwise the same: it is still a thread-affine, in-process lock and you still cannot await inside it. For async code the tool remains `SemaphoreSlim` with `WaitAsync`.
questions.asked: A currency question; the strong answer adds that async critical sections still need SemaphoreSlim.

questions.q: What does this print (C# 12)?
choices: It does not compile: `..a` is range syntax, not a spread
questions.why: Collection expressions build any target collection type from literal elements, and `..a` spreads the elements of `a` in place, like `...a` in JavaScript. So `b` holds 1, 2, 1, 2, 3; reading `..a` as one nested element gives the tempting 3. The target type decides what gets built, which is why the same `[..]` syntax works for arrays, lists and spans.
questions.asked: An easy currency check for C# 12, and the JavaScript spread analogy helps full-stack candidates.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: one: 4
It does not compile: `..` is valid only in a range
questions.why: List patterns (C# 11) match on shape: `[]` is empty, `[var only]` is exactly one element, and `[var first, .., var last]` is two or more, where `..` is a slice pattern matching any number of middle elements. Three elements hit the last arm and bind 4 and 6. The switch arms are tried in order.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know modern pattern matching beyond type checks.

questions.q: What does `[NotNullWhen(true)]` change for the caller?
choices: The compiler treats `n` as non-null inside the if, so `n.Length` raises no warning
It throws an ArgumentNullException if the method returns true while name is still null
The compiler demands an explicit null check on `n` before every use inside the if
It changes the out type to `string`, so no caller can ever receive a null value
questions.why: Nullable flow attributes tell the compiler how nullability depends on the return value; `Dictionary.TryGetValue` uses exactly this. Without the attribute, `n` stays `string?` in the if and `n.Length` warns. Like all NRT annotations it has no runtime effect, so it checks nothing if the method lies.
questions.asked: Shows you write APIs that work with the nullable analysis instead of sprinkling `!` at call sites.

questions.q: Inside an async method, why use `await Task.Delay(1000)` rather than `Thread.Sleep(1000)`?
choices: Task.Delay is more precise, while Thread.Sleep can drift by several seconds
Thread.Sleep holds the thread for the whole second; Task.Delay frees it
Thread.Sleep cannot be used inside an async method and does not compile there
Task.Delay runs the rest of the method on a brand new dedicated thread from the pool
questions.why: `Thread.Sleep` holds a thread doing nothing, which on a server means one fewer thread-pool thread for other requests. `await Task.Delay` registers a timer and returns the thread; the continuation is scheduled when it fires. Sleep compiles fine inside async code, which is why it slips through review.
questions.asked: The simplest test of whether you understand what await actually saves.

questions.q: Does marking a method `async` make it run on a background thread?
choices: Yes, the compiler wraps the whole method body in a call to Task.Run
Yes, but only when the method returns Task<T> rather than a plain Task
No, it runs on the caller's thread until the first incomplete await
No, async methods always run on the UI or request thread for their whole life
questions.why: `async` just lets you use `await` and builds a state machine. The body runs synchronously on the calling thread up to the first await of an incomplete task; the rest runs as a continuation, on the thread pool in ASP.NET Core. CPU-bound code before that await blocks the caller. Only `Task.Run` explicitly moves work to another thread.
questions.asked: A foundational misconception; interviewers listen for "synchronously until the first await".

questions.q: `GetUserAsync()` and `GetOrdersAsync()` each take about 1 second and are independent. Roughly how long does this take?
questions.code:
var user = await GetUserAsync(id);
var orders = await GetOrdersAsync(id);
choices: About 1 second, because both awaits overlap on the thread pool
About 2 seconds, because the second call starts after the first ends
About 0 seconds, because await returns to the caller immediately
About 1 second on .NET 9, and 2 seconds on older runtimes
questions.why: Each await suspends the method until that call completes, so the calls run one after another. To overlap them, start both first and then await: `var u = GetUserAsync(id); var o = GetOrdersAsync(id); await Task.WhenAll(u, o);`. With EF Core, keep in mind one DbContext cannot run two queries at once.
questions.asked: The quickest real-world latency win in async code; the DbContext caveat is what a strong candidate adds.

questions.q: What does `await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3)` return when the tasks are `Task<int>`?
choices: An int[] with results in the order the tasks were passed
An int[] with results in the order the tasks completed
The single result of whichever of the three tasks finished last
A Task<int>[] that you still need to await one by one
questions.why: `WhenAll` over `Task<T>` produces a `T[]` whose positions match the argument order, regardless of which finished first. If any task faults, awaiting it throws the first exception; the rest are on the returned task's `Exception`. For completion order use `Task.WhenEach` (.NET 9).
questions.asked: Basic API knowledge; confusion about ordering causes subtle mismatches between inputs and results.

questions.q: An interface declares `Task<Product?> FindAsync(int id)`. Your in-memory test double has the answer immediately. What should it return?
choices: `Task.Run(() => _items.GetValueOrDefault(id))`
`Task.FromResult(_items.GetValueOrDefault(id))`
`new Task<Product?>(() => _items.GetValueOrDefault(id))`
`Task.CompletedTask`, followed by the product as an out parameter
questions.why: `Task.FromResult` wraps an already known value in a completed task with no thread hop. `Task.Run` wastes a pool thread, and `new Task(...)` creates a cold task that never starts, so awaiting it hangs forever. Marking the method async and returning the value also works, with a small state-machine cost.
questions.asked: Common in fakes and caches; the cold-task trap with `new Task` is a nice extra.

questions.q: In an ASP.NET Core controller, what does wrapping an EF Core query in `await Task.Run(() => db.Orders.ToList())` achieve?
choices: It makes the request faster, because the query runs in parallel with the action
It frees the request thread, which improves scalability under heavy load
Nothing useful: it swaps one pool thread for another that blocks
It prevents the DbContext from being used by two threads at the same time
questions.why: ASP.NET Core already runs on the thread pool, so Task.Run just moves blocking work to a different pool thread, with extra overhead. The real fix is the true async API, `await db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct)`, which releases the thread during I/O. Task.Run is for CPU-bound work in UI apps, not I/O on servers.
questions.asked: A very common anti-pattern called "fake async"; interviewers want you to name it.

questions.q: In a desktop or console app, when is `Task.Run` the right tool?
choices: To offload CPU-heavy work, such as resizing images, so the UI thread stays responsive
To make any I/O call asynchronous when the library offers no async API of its own
To run database queries faster by splitting them across several pool threads
To guarantee the work runs on the main thread after the current method returns
questions.why: Task.Run queues a delegate to the thread pool, which is what you want for CPU-bound work that would otherwise freeze a UI thread. Wrapping synchronous I/O only hides blocking on another thread. It never runs work on the main thread.
questions.asked: Paired with the ASP.NET question to check you know Task.Run's legitimate use.

questions.q: Why does this method dispose the client too early?
choices: It does not: a using declaration waits for the returned task before it disposes
HttpClient disposes itself after each request, so the using is redundant
The using is ignored when the method returns a Task, so the client leaks instead
The method returns as soon as the request starts, disposing the client early
questions.why: Without `async`/`await`, the method returns the in-flight task immediately and the using declaration disposes the client on the way out, cancelling the request with an ObjectDisposedException or TaskCanceledException. Mark it `async` and `return await ...` so disposal waits. (Also inject `IHttpClientFactory` rather than creating clients.)
questions.asked: The classic danger of eliding async; interviewers want "only elide when there is no using or try around it".

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: `lock` only accepts a string key, not an object field
`await` is banned in a lock, since the method may resume on another thread
SaveAsync must be called with ConfigureAwait(false) inside a lock
`lock` blocks may contain only synchronous statements that return void, not tasks
questions.why: A Monitor lock is owned by a thread, and after an await the method may resume on a different thread, so releasing it would be wrong; the compiler reports CS1996. Use `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` with `await WaitAsync()` and `Release()` in a finally for async mutual exclusion.
questions.asked: Leads straight into how you do async locking, which interviewers then ask about.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
choices: If UpdateCacheAsync throws, Release never runs and every later caller waits forever
WaitAsync must be called without await, or the semaphore deadlocks on the first caller
A SemaphoreSlim with a count of 1 cannot be used across async calls
Release must be called before the awaited work, not after it
questions.why: Without try/finally, an exception skips `Release()` and the semaphore stays at zero, so the next `WaitAsync` hangs. The fix is `await gate.WaitAsync(); try { ... } finally { gate.Release(); }`. SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) is the standard async mutex.
questions.asked: A realistic hang in production; the try/finally is the expected fix.

questions.q: What is the problem with `orders.ForEach(async o => await SendEmailAsync(o));`?
choices: ForEach runs all the lambdas in parallel, which overloads the mail server
ForEach awaits each lambda, so the emails are sent too slowly
The lambda is async void, so ForEach cannot wait and errors are lost
It does not compile, because ForEach does not accept async lambdas
questions.why: `List<T>.ForEach` takes an `Action<T>`, so the async lambda compiles as `async void`. ForEach returns immediately after starting each call, the caller cannot await completion, and an exception can crash the process. Use a normal `foreach` with await, or `Task.WhenAll` / `Parallel.ForEachAsync` for concurrency.
questions.asked: Async void hiding in a lambda is a favourite code-review catch.

questions.q: What does `Parallel.ForEachAsync` (.NET 6) give you over `Task.WhenAll(items.Select(ProcessAsync))`?
choices: It runs every item on its own dedicated OS thread
It returns results in completion order instead of input order
It retries failed items automatically before throwing
A built-in cap on concurrency through MaxDegreeOfParallelism
questions.why: `WhenAll` over a Select starts every operation at once, which can mean thousands of simultaneous HTTP calls. `Parallel.ForEachAsync(items, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 }, async (item, ct) => ...)` processes items with at most eight in flight and passes a cancellation token. It returns no results; collect them yourself if needed.
questions.asked: Throttling concurrent calls to a rate-limited API is a practical need.

questions.q: What does `await task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))` (.NET 6) do if the task is still running after 5 seconds?
choices: It cancels the underlying operation and then throws OperationCanceledException
It throws TimeoutException, but the underlying operation keeps running
It returns default(T) and lets the operation continue in the background
It blocks the thread until the task finishes, however long that takes
questions.why: `WaitAsync` stops waiting, not the work: after the timeout it throws `TimeoutException`, and the original task carries on unless you also cancel it via a token. For real cancellation pass a token with `CancelAfter` to the operation itself. It replaces the old `Task.WhenAny(task, Task.Delay(...))` pattern.
questions.asked: Separates "stop waiting" from "stop working", a subtle but important distinction.

questions.q: How do you cancel an outgoing call when either the client disconnects or 10 seconds pass?
choices: This does not work: CancelAfter replaces the linked token with a new one
This works, but only if http.Timeout is also set to exactly 10 seconds
This cancels only on disconnect; CancelAfter applies to the next call
This works: the linked source fires on disconnect or when the timer ends
questions.why: A linked token source is cancelled when any source token is cancelled or when it is cancelled itself, here by the `CancelAfter` timer. Disposing it (the using) unregisters it from the parent. `HttpClient.Timeout` is a separate, client-wide limit.
questions.asked: Combining request abort with a per-call timeout is a common pattern in API code.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core action catches every exception and logs it as an error. Why do logs fill up with `TaskCanceledException` errors?
choices: TaskCanceledException is thrown whenever a query returns no rows
EF Core throws it on every SaveChangesAsync call that has no changes
Disconnected clients cancel RequestAborted, so pending awaits throw
The thread pool cancels any task that runs longer than the default 30 seconds
questions.why: When a client goes away, `HttpContext.RequestAborted` fires and any awaited call using it throws `OperationCanceledException` (TaskCanceledException derives from it). That is expected, not an error. Filter it: `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)` and log at a lower level.
questions.asked: Real log-noise problem; strong answers know TaskCanceledException derives from OperationCanceledException.

questions.q: In a minimal API endpoint, how do you get a token that fires when the client disconnects?
choices: Add a `CancellationToken` parameter; it is bound to HttpContext.RequestAborted
Create a `new CancellationTokenSource()` at the start of the handler
Read it from IConfiguration under the key "RequestAborted"
Call `Task.Delay(Timeout.Infinite)` and await it alongside the work
questions.why: Minimal APIs and controllers bind a `CancellationToken` parameter to `HttpContext.RequestAborted` automatically. Pass it down to EF Core and HttpClient calls so abandoned requests stop using the database. A fresh CancellationTokenSource is never cancelled by anything.
questions.asked: Basic plumbing that shows you think about wasted work on abandoned requests.

questions.q: What happens to an exception thrown inside `SendAsync` here?
questions.code:
_ = SendAsync(order);   // fire and forget
return Results.Ok();
choices: It is rethrown in the request pipeline and turned into a 500 response
It crashes the process immediately, like an unhandled exception on a thread
It is stored in the discarded task and never observed or logged
It is retried automatically by the thread pool up to three times
questions.why: The exception is captured in the returned Task, and since nobody awaits it, it is silently lost (at most raising `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` on finalisation). Fire-and-forget work should go to a queue processed by a hosted service, which can log and retry. It does not crash the process, unlike async void.
questions.asked: Explains "the email never sent and there is no error" incidents.

questions.q: Why do experienced developers create `new TaskCompletionSource<T>(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously)`?
choices: It makes SetResult throw if the task has already been completed once
It lets the task be awaited more than once, like a ValueTask
It starts the task on a thread-pool thread as soon as it is created
It stops awaiting code from running inline inside the SetResult call
questions.why: By default, `SetResult` can run awaiting continuations synchronously on the caller's thread, so the code that completes the task suddenly executes someone else's logic, possibly while holding a lock, which can cause deadlocks or stack dives. The option forces continuations onto the thread pool.
questions.asked: Deep async knowledge; it usually comes up when discussing custom awaitable coordination code.

questions.q: What does `AsyncLocal<T>` do?
choices: Stores a value per thread, like ThreadStatic, and resets it at each await
Stores a value that flows with the async call chain, across awaits and threads
Stores a value in the HTTP response headers for the current request
Stores a value globally but locks it during each asynchronous operation
questions.why: AsyncLocal values travel with the ExecutionContext, so they follow an async flow even when continuations resume on different threads; changes made in a child flow do not leak back to the parent. `IHttpContextAccessor` and logging scopes are built on it. `[ThreadStatic]` breaks across awaits.
questions.asked: Explains how ambient context like HttpContext or activity tracing works; a strong answer warns against overusing it.

questions.q: Which is the idiomatic way to run work every 30 seconds inside a `BackgroundService` in .NET 6+?
choices: A `PeriodicTimer` awaited with `while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(ct))`
`while (true) { DoWork(); Thread.Sleep(30_000); }` inside the ExecuteAsync method
`new System.Timers.Timer(30_000)` with an async void Elapsed handler
A static constructor that starts a dedicated thread which loops forever with a sleep
questions.why: `PeriodicTimer` gives an awaitable tick that respects cancellation and never overlaps runs, because the next tick is awaited only after your work finishes. Thread.Sleep blocks a pool thread and ignores shutdown, and an async void timer handler can overlap and lose exceptions.
questions.asked: Recurring jobs are common; this checks you know the modern, cancellation-friendly primitive.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: caught only, because the throw happens at Check(-1)
created, then caught
created only, because the exception is lost
An unhandled ArgumentException at Check(-1)
questions.why: In an `async` method, even an exception thrown before the first await is captured in the returned Task rather than thrown from the call. So `created` prints, and the exception surfaces when `t` is awaited. If you want argument errors thrown eagerly, validate in a non-async wrapper.
questions.asked: Tests precise knowledge of how async methods package exceptions.

questions.q: For a new public method that performs I/O, which return type is the recommended default?
choices: `ValueTask<T>`, because it is always faster and allocates less than Task<T>
`Task<T>`, unless profiling shows a hot, mostly synchronous path
`void`, with an event raised when the operation completes
`IAsyncResult`, the classic asynchronous programming model
questions.why: `Task<T>` has no consumption restrictions: you can await it many times, store it, or pass it to WhenAll. `ValueTask<T>` avoids an allocation only when results are often synchronous, such as cache hits, and has single-await rules. IAsyncResult is the obsolete Begin/End pattern.
questions.asked: Shows judgement: using ValueTask everywhere is a red flag, not a sign of expertise.

questions.q: Can you use `await` inside `catch` and `finally` blocks?
choices: No, the compiler rejects await in both catch and finally blocks
Only in finally, because a catch block must finish synchronously
Only in catch, because a finally block cannot contain asynchronous work
Yes, it has been allowed in both since C# 6
questions.why: C# 6 lifted the restriction, so you can `await LogAsync(ex)` in a catch or `await conn.CloseAsync()` in a finally. The restriction that remains is await inside a `lock` statement.
questions.asked: Short knowledge check; older tutorials still claim it is not allowed.

questions.q: Why can `ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd(key, k => CreateExpensive(k))` still call `CreateExpensive` twice for the same key?
choices: The factory runs outside the lock, so racing threads may each run it
GetOrAdd is not thread-safe, so it should only be called from a single thread
The dictionary clears its cache every time it resizes, so the value must be recreated
The factory runs on every call, and GetOrAdd only decides which result to return
questions.why: ConcurrentDictionary keeps the dictionary consistent but runs your factory without holding a lock, so concurrent misses can both invoke it; one value wins and the other is discarded. If the factory must run once, store `Lazy<T>` values: `GetOrAdd(key, k => new Lazy<T>(() => Create(k))).Value`.
questions.asked: A well-known subtlety; the Lazy<T> fix is the answer interviewers are waiting for.

questions.q: A singleton service keeps a `List<string>` of recent searches and calls `Add` from every request. What can go wrong?
choices: Nothing, since each request runs on its own thread with its own copy of the list
Nothing, because List<T>.Add takes an internal lock before writing
Concurrent Adds can corrupt it or throw, since List<T> is not thread-safe
The list is recreated per request, so the searches are simply lost
questions.why: A singleton is shared by all concurrent requests, and `List<T>` has no internal locking; simultaneous `Add` calls can overwrite each other or leave it inconsistent (IndexOutOfRangeException during resize). Use a lock, `ConcurrentQueue<T>`, or a thread-safe cache. Scoped or transient services avoid the sharing altogether.
questions.asked: Shared mutable state in singletons is one of the top real-world ASP.NET bugs.

questions.q: Why is `_count++` unsafe when many threads run it, and what is the cheap fix?
choices: ++ on an int is atomic, but it can overflow; use a long counter instead
++ is read, add, write, so updates can be lost; use Interlocked.Increment
++ is slow under contention; mark the field volatile so the CPU can cache the value
++ can throw under contention; wrap it in a try/catch and retry the increment
questions.why: Two threads can read the same value and both write back value + 1, losing an increment. `Interlocked.Increment` does the read-modify-write atomically without a lock. `volatile` only affects visibility and reordering; it does not make ++ atomic.
questions.asked: A fundamentals-of-concurrency question with a precise one-line fix.

questions.q: What does a bounded `Channel<T>` (System.Threading.Channels) give a producer/consumer pipeline?
choices: Persistent storage, so queued jobs survive a process restart
Delivery of every job to every consumer that is reading from the channel at the time
An async queue whose writers wait once 100 items are pending
A lock-free list that sorts the pending jobs by their priority
questions.why: Channels are in-memory async queues. With a bound, `WriteAsync` waits when the buffer is full, so a fast producer cannot exhaust memory; readers await items without polling. Each item goes to one reader. It is in-memory only, so jobs are lost on restart; use a durable queue when that matters.
questions.asked: The standard building block for in-process background queues in ASP.NET Core.

questions.q: What does `Task.Factory.StartNew(async () => await WorkAsync())` return, and why is that a trap?
choices: A Task<Task>, so one await only waits for WorkAsync to start
A Task that completes when WorkAsync completes, exactly like the Task.Run overload
A ValueTask, which may only be awaited once
A cold Task that never starts unless you call Start
questions.why: StartNew does not understand async delegates, so the outer task completes as soon as the lambda returns its inner Task. You would need `.Unwrap()` or a double await. `Task.Run` has overloads for `Func<Task>` that unwrap automatically, which is why it is preferred.
questions.asked: Explains mysterious "completed too early" bugs in older code.

questions.q: An ASP.NET Core app under load shows low CPU, a growing thread count, and requests that take seconds even for trivial endpoints. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The garbage collector is running too often because of large JSON responses
The database connection string is missing its Pooling=true setting
Kestrel limits concurrent connections to the number of CPU cores by default
Thread-pool starvation from sync-over-async code such as .Result or .Wait()
questions.why: Blocking on tasks ties up pool threads while they wait; the pool injects new threads slowly, so queued work, including the continuations those blocked threads are waiting for, sits idle. Low CPU with high latency and a climbing thread count is the signature. `dotnet-counters` shows the thread-pool queue length.
questions.asked: A diagnosis question; naming the symptoms and the counters shows production experience.

questions.q: What is `Program.Main` allowed to look like in a console app since C# 7.1?
choices: It must be `static void Main`, and async work has to call .Wait()
It can be `static async Task Main` or `static async Task<int> Main`
It can be `static async void Main`, which the runtime awaits
It must be an instance method on a class called App
questions.why: An async Main returning `Task` or `Task<int>` lets you await directly; the compiler generates a synchronous entry point that waits for it. With top-level statements, using await makes the generated Main async automatically. `async void Main` would exit before the work finishes.
questions.asked: Basic, but it explains why older samples call .GetAwaiter().GetResult() in Main.

questions.q: In .NET 10, what does `customers.LeftJoin(orders, c => c.Id, o => o.CustomerId, (c, o) => new { c.Name, Total = o?.Total })` return for a customer with no orders?
choices: Nothing: customers without a match are dropped, as with Join
One row with the customer's name and a null Total
A row per order in the system, each with a null name
It throws, because `o` is never allowed to be null
questions.why: .NET 10 added `LeftJoin` and `RightJoin` to LINQ, and EF Core 10 translates them to SQL LEFT/RIGHT JOIN. Unmatched outer elements appear once with the inner element set to null. Before .NET 10 you wrote `GroupJoin` followed by `SelectMany(... .DefaultIfEmpty())`, which is still what you will see in older code.
questions.asked: Tests currency with .NET 10, and whether you can explain the old GroupJoin pattern it replaces.

questions.q: What does `Join` do with an order whose CustomerId matches no customer?
questions.code: var rows = orders.Join(customers, o => o.CustomerId, c => c.Id, (o, c) => new { o.Id, c.Name });
choices: It includes the order with Name set to null
It throws KeyNotFoundException for that order
It includes the order with an empty Name
It leaves the order out of the result
questions.why: `Join` is an inner join: only pairs with equal keys are produced, so orphaned orders vanish silently. That can make report totals quietly wrong. Use `LeftJoin` (.NET 10) or GroupJoin with DefaultIfEmpty when unmatched rows must stay.
questions.asked: Same inner-versus-outer join reasoning as SQL, applied to in-memory data.

questions.q: What is the difference between `a.Concat(b)` and `a.Union(b)`?
choices: Concat keeps duplicates; Union removes them using default equality
Concat sorts the combined result; Union keeps the original order
Concat runs eagerly; Union is deferred until enumeration
Concat requires both sequences to be of the same length
questions.why: `Concat` appends b after a exactly as they are, like SQL UNION ALL. `Union` yields distinct elements from both, like SQL UNION, using the default equality comparer (or `UnionBy` with a key). Both are deferred and neither sorts.
questions.asked: Maps LINQ onto SQL set operations, which interviewers often probe together.

questions.q: You have yesterday's and today's lists of product SKUs. Which call finds SKUs that were removed today?
choices: `today.Except(yesterday)`
`yesterday.Intersect(today)`
`yesterday.Except(today)`
`today.Union(yesterday)`
questions.why: `a.Except(b)` yields the distinct elements of a that are not in b, so removed SKUs are those in yesterday but not today. `today.Except(yesterday)` gives the added ones, and Intersect gives the unchanged ones. Except uses a hash set internally, so it is O(n + m).
questions.asked: Diffing two lists is common in sync jobs and imports.

questions.q: Which call returns the whole `Product` with the highest price, not just the price?
choices: `products.Max(p => p.Price)`
`products.OrderBy(p => p.Price).First()`
`products.MaxBy(p => p.Price)`
`products.Select(p => p.Price).Last()`
questions.why: `MaxBy` (.NET 6) returns the element with the largest key in one pass. `Max(selector)` returns the price itself, and OrderBy then First sorts everything and picks the cheapest. Before .NET 6 people used OrderByDescending then First, which is O(n log n).
questions.asked: A small modern-API question with a performance angle.

questions.q: Page numbers start at 1 and each page has `size` items. Which expression returns page `page`?
choices: `items.Skip(page * size).Take(size)`
`items.Skip((page - 1) * size).Take(size)`
`items.Take(size).Skip((page - 1) * size)`
`items.Skip(page).Take(size)`
questions.why: Page 1 must skip zero items, so the offset is `(page - 1) * size`. Taking before skipping would produce an empty page for page 2 onwards. Against a database, add a deterministic OrderBy first, or pages can overlap.
questions.asked: Every CRUD list endpoint needs paging; the off-by-one and ordering caveats are the point.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: `Aggregate` with a seed starts the accumulator at 100 and applies the function to each element in order: 100 - 10 - 20 - 5 = 65. It is LINQ's version of JavaScript's `reduce` with an initial value. Without a seed the first element becomes the accumulator, and an empty sequence throws.
questions.asked: Knowing Aggregate as reduce helps JavaScript developers read functional C#.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: `==` gives True and SequenceEqual gives True
`==` gives False and SequenceEqual gives True
`==` gives False and SequenceEqual gives False
`==` gives True and SequenceEqual gives False
questions.why: Arrays are reference types without an overloaded `==`, so two separate arrays are not equal. `SequenceEqual` compares element by element in order. Collections inside records are compared the same way as `==` here, which is why records holding lists do not behave like values.
questions.asked: A basic equality check that trips up people who expect value semantics for collections.

questions.q: What does `lookup["missing"]` return when `lookup` came from `orders.ToLookup(o => o.Region)`?
choices: An empty sequence; ILookup never throws for a missing key
null, because that key has no group in the lookup at all
It throws KeyNotFoundException, exactly like a Dictionary
A sequence holding a single default(Order) element
questions.why: `ILookup<TKey, TElement>` returns an empty sequence for an unknown key, which makes it convenient for one-to-many lookups in loops. `ToLookup` is eager, unlike `GroupBy`, so build it once and reuse it rather than calling Where inside a loop.
questions.asked: ToLookup is the tidy fix for N-squared Where-inside-a-loop code.

questions.q: When is the `FormatException` thrown?
questions.code:
var raw = new[] { "1", "x", "3" };
var nums = raw.Select(int.Parse);      // line A
var list = nums.Where(n => n > 0);    // line B
var arr = list.ToArray();             // line C
choices: At line A, where int.Parse is passed to Select
At line B, when the filter is attached
At line C, when the pipeline is enumerated
It is never thrown; bad items are skipped
questions.why: Select and Where are deferred, so nothing is parsed until `ToArray` enumerates. The stack trace then points at line C, which can mislead you if the query was built in another method. Validate or use TryParse inside the projection when input can be bad.
questions.asked: Explains why exceptions from LINQ appear far from the lambda that caused them.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: null, then -1
0, then -1
0, then 0
It throws InvalidOperationException
questions.why: For a value type the default is `default(int)`, 0, which is indistinguishable from a real 0 in the data. .NET 6 added overloads that take the fallback value, so the second line prints -1. For reference types the default is null.
questions.asked: The ambiguous-zero problem is a real bug source; knowing the newer overload is a nice touch.

questions.q: What does `.DefaultIfEmpty(0)` do in `orders.Select(o => o.Total).DefaultIfEmpty(0).Max()`?
choices: It replaces every zero total with the default value
It filters out orders whose Total is zero
It makes Max return null for an empty sequence
It yields a single 0 when there are no orders, so Max does not throw
questions.why: `DefaultIfEmpty(x)` passes the sequence through unchanged if it has elements, or yields just x if it is empty. Max over a non-empty sequence never throws, so the report shows 0 instead of crashing. Against EF Core, projecting to `(decimal?)o.Total` and using `?? 0` translates more reliably.
questions.asked: A clean fix for aggregate-on-empty errors in dashboards.

questions.q: What does this custom operator do, and when does its loop run?
choices: It filters out nulls eagerly, building a new list when called
It filters out nulls lazily, one element at a time as the caller enumerates
It throws on the first null element it meets while enumerating
It replaces nulls with default(T) and returns every element
questions.why: An extension method with `yield return` is how LINQ operators are written: nothing runs until enumeration, and elements stream through one at a time. Combined with the `where T : class` constraint, the return type drops the `?`, so callers get non-null elements with no warnings.
questions.asked: Writing a small LINQ-style operator shows you understand iterators, extensions and generics together.

questions.q: When can `AsParallel()` make a LINQ-to-objects query slower rather than faster?
choices: When per-item work is tiny, so partitioning costs more than it saves
When the source sequence has more than about 1,000 elements in it
Only on machines that have fewer than four physical processor cores
When the query contains a Where clause placed before the Select
questions.why: PLINQ splits the input across threads and merges the results, which only pays off when each element needs meaningful CPU work. For cheap projections it is slower, the order is not preserved without `AsOrdered()`, and on a server it competes with requests for pool threads. It does nothing for I/O-bound work.
questions.asked: Tests judgement: people reach for AsParallel as a magic speed-up.

questions.q: What does `source.TryGetNonEnumeratedCount(out var n)` (.NET 6) tell you?
choices: The count of a lazy query, by running it once and caching the result
Whether the source is empty, without evaluating the query
The count if it is known without enumerating, e.g. for a List or array
The number of times the source has been enumerated so far
questions.why: It returns true and the count when the source can report it cheaply (it implements ICollection or is a LINQ operator that knows its size), and false otherwise. It never enumerates. It is useful for pre-sizing a buffer without triggering a query twice.
questions.asked: A niche API; it tests whether you think about accidental enumeration.

questions.q: What does `Enumerable.Range(1, 5)` produce?
questions.why: The parameters are the start and the count, not the end, so you get five numbers starting at 1. It is handy for seed data and test fixtures, such as `Enumerable.Range(1, 50).Select(i => new Product($"P{i}"))`.
questions.asked: A small detail that often causes off-by-one bugs in seed data.

questions.q: In LINQ to objects, where do elements with a null key go in `people.OrderBy(p => p.Nickname)`?
choices: First, because the default comparer treats null as smaller than any string
Last, because nulls are always sorted after real values
They are removed from the result
It throws ArgumentNullException when it meets a null key
questions.why: `Comparer<string>.Default` orders null before every non-null value, so nulls come first ascending and last descending. SQL databases differ: SQL Server sorts NULLs first ascending, Postgres sorts them last. Results can change when a query moves between memory and the database.
questions.asked: Explains ordering differences between in-memory tests and the real database.

questions.q: Why can this generic method not be called as `var n = Parse("42");`?
questions.code: static T Parse<T>(string s) where T : IParsable<T> => T.Parse(s, null);
choices: Static abstract interface members cannot be used from generic methods
IParsable<T> is only available in preview language versions
The method must be async, because parsing may be slow
C# cannot infer T from a return type, so you must write Parse<int>("42")
questions.why: Type inference only uses the arguments, and the only argument is a string, so T is unknown; you write `Parse<int>("42")`. `IParsable<T>` (.NET 7) is a stable interface with a static abstract `Parse`, which is exactly what generic math and this constraint allow.
questions.asked: Explains a common compiler complaint when writing generic helpers.

questions.q: What does `where T : IEntity` let you do inside `class Repository<T> where T : IEntity`?
choices: Access members declared on IEntity, such as `item.Id`, on any T
Create new instances of T anywhere in the class with `new T()`
Store every T as a value type, which avoids boxing on each call
Compare two T values directly with the built-in == operator
questions.why: An interface constraint means every T implements IEntity, so the compiler lets you call its members. `new T()` needs the `new()` constraint, and `==` on T needs an operator available through a constraint, such as `IEqualityOperators<T, T, bool>`, or `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`.
questions.asked: The standard generic-repository shape; interviewers use it to check constraint basics.

questions.q: Why does `if (a == b)` fail to compile inside `bool Same<T>(T a, T b)` with no constraints?
choices: Generic methods cannot compare parameters at all
T might be a struct without an == operator, so the compiler has none to call
== is only defined for string and the numeric types
The method must be marked static for == to be available
questions.why: With no constraints the compiler cannot know which `==` to use, so it refuses (CS0019). Use `EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals(a, b)`, which respects IEquatable<T> and overridden Equals. With `where T : class`, `==` compiles but means reference equality, which is often not what you want.
questions.asked: A classic generic-code puzzle; EqualityComparer<T>.Default is the idiomatic answer.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: Each closed generic type, `Counter<int>` and `Counter<string>`, is a distinct type with its own static fields. That is useful for per-type caches (like `EqualityComparer<T>.Default`) and surprising if you expected one shared counter.
questions.asked: Explains per-type static caches, which show up in serialisers and mapping libraries.

questions.q: Why does this assignment compile?
questions.code:
IComparer<Animal> byName = Comparer<Animal>.Create((x, y) => string.Compare(x.Name, y.Name));
IComparer<Dog> dogs = byName;
choices: IComparer<in T> is contravariant: something that compares any Animal can compare Dogs
IComparer<out T> is covariant, so a comparer of a base type can become a derived one
Dog inherits from Animal, so every generic type of Animal converts to one of Dog
The compiler inserts a cast that is checked at runtime for each comparison
questions.why: `in T` marks T as input-only, so a consumer of the base type can stand in for a consumer of the derived type. `IEnumerable<out T>` is the opposite: producers of Dog can be used as producers of Animal. Classes such as `List<T>` are invariant, so neither conversion applies to them.
questions.asked: Variance questions separate people who memorised `in`/`out` from those who can reason about them.

questions.q: What does the `where T : struct` constraint let you write that an unconstrained T does not?
choices: `new T[10]`, an array of ten elements of the type
`T?` meaning `Nullable<T>`, with HasValue and Value
`T.Parse(text)` for any value type, including enums
`lock (value)` on a parameter of type T inside the method
questions.why: With the struct constraint, `T?` is `Nullable<T>`, so you can return 'no value' for ints, dates or enums. Arrays of any T are always allowed, `lock` needs a reference type, and static members like Parse need an interface constraint such as `IParsable<T>`.
questions.asked: Shows you understand how nullability differs between value and reference types in generic code.

questions.q: What does `where TEnum : struct, Enum` let a helper do?
questions.code: static string[] Names<TEnum>() where TEnum : struct, Enum => Enum.GetNames<TEnum>();
choices: Accept only enum types at compile time, so Names<int>() is rejected
Convert any value type to an enum at runtime
Treat every enum as a [Flags] enum automatically
Call the method without specifying TEnum at all
questions.why: Since C# 7.3 you can constrain to `System.Enum`; adding `struct` excludes the `Enum` base class itself. Callers can only pass enum types, and generic APIs like `Enum.GetNames<TEnum>()` or `Enum.Parse<TEnum>` work without typeof or casting.
questions.asked: Handy for dropdown or validation helpers over enums.

questions.q: How do you register a generic repository once for every entity type in ASP.NET Core DI?
choices: `services.AddScoped<IRepository<object>, Repository<object>>();`
`services.AddScoped(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(Repository<>));`
`services.AddScoped<IRepository, Repository>();` with reflection inside
One `AddScoped` call per entity; open generics are not supported
questions.why: The container supports open generic registrations: when something asks for `IRepository<Order>`, it closes `Repository<>` over Order. Registering `<object>` would give every consumer an object repository, and generic interfaces are invariant so it would not even resolve.
questions.asked: Common in real codebases; the typeof syntax is what they want to see.

questions.q: In a generic method with no constraint on T (C# 9+), what does a return type of `T?` mean?
choices: For value types it always becomes Nullable<T>, for classes a nullable reference
It is a compile error unless T is constrained to class
The method may return default(T): null for reference types, zero-like for value types
The method always returns null for value types, boxed as object
questions.why: For an unconstrained T, `T?` is a nullability annotation meaning "may be default". For `int` it stays `int`, not `int?`, so a caller gets 0, and for `string` it is `string?`. This is how `FirstOrDefault<T>` is annotated. Only `where T : struct` turns T? into Nullable<T>.
questions.asked: A subtle rule that explains surprising results from generic Try/Find helpers.

questions.q: When should you write a generic method instead of one that takes `object`?
choices: Never; object parameters are simpler and just as fast
When the method must accept exactly one specific type
Only when the method is going to be used from JavaScript
When you want type safety and no boxing across many types
questions.why: A generic method keeps the caller's type, so there are no casts, mismatches become compile errors, and value types are not boxed. `object` parameters push type checks to runtime. `List<T>` replaced the old `ArrayList` for exactly these reasons.
questions.asked: A foundations question; ArrayList versus List<T> is the classic example.

questions.q: What does `Zip` produce here?
choices: Ann:90 Bob:75 Cy:0
Ann:90 Bob:75
It throws, because the sequences differ in length
Ann:90 Bob:75 Cy:
questions.why: `Zip` pairs elements by position and stops when the shorter sequence ends, so Cy is dropped without an error. Since .NET Core 3.0 the overload without a selector returns tuples, which deconstruct nicely. Check lengths yourself if a mismatch indicates bad data.
questions.asked: Pairing parallel arrays is common in import code; the silent truncation is the gotcha.

questions.q: What does the index overload of `Select` give you here?
questions.code: var lines = items.Select((item, i) => $"{i + 1}. {item}");
choices: The item and its zero-based position in the source
The item and the total number of items in the source
The item and a hash of its value
The item and its one-based position in the source
questions.why: `Select((x, i) => ...)` passes the zero-based index alongside each element, which is why the code adds 1 for a numbered list. .NET 9 also added `Index()`, which yields `(int Index, T Item)` tuples.
questions.asked: Numbered output and position-aware transforms are everyday tasks.

questions.q: What is the difference between a generic method and a generic class?
choices: A generic class can only have one type parameter; methods can have many
A generic method's T is chosen per call; a generic class's T is fixed for each instance
Generic methods are resolved at runtime; generic classes at compile time
A generic method must be static, while a generic class cannot be
questions.why: `Box<T>` fixes T for the whole instance, so every member shares it. `static T Clamp<T>(...)` picks T per call, usually by inference. Both are resolved by the compiler and specialised by the JIT, and both can have several type parameters.
questions.asked: Basic vocabulary; the per-call versus per-instance distinction is the answer.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: True, because `==` on Animal compares only the Name
It does not compile: Dog's Name hides the base property
True for `==`, but `a.Equals(b)` returns False
False, because record equality also compares runtime type
questions.why: Records generate a virtual `EqualityContract` property that returns the runtime type, and `Equals` compares it before any members. A Dog is never equal to a plain Animal even when the shared members match. `==` just calls `Equals`, so the two always agree.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know record equality is type-aware, which matters when records form a hierarchy of events or messages.

questions.q: What does `Console.WriteLine(new Point(1, 2));` print for `record Point(int X, int Y);`?
choices: Point(1, 2)
Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }
Point { X: 1, Y: 2 }
questions.why: Records synthesise a `ToString` that prints the type name and each public property as `Name = value` in braces, which makes them pleasant in logs and test failures. It is not JSON; a plain class would print only its full type name.
questions.asked: A quick check that you have actually used records, and a hint that you like readable logs.

questions.q: Since C# 10, which types can you use a `with` expression on?
choices: Only record classes, because `with` relies on the generated clone method
Any class or struct whose properties are all declared as init-only
Records, any struct, and anonymous types, but not ordinary classes
Any type that implements ICloneable, including ordinary classes
questions.why: `with` works on record classes (via a hidden clone method), on every struct including record structs (a struct copy is already a clone), and on anonymous types. A plain class, even one with only `init` properties, has no clone method, so `with` does not compile; ICloneable plays no part.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know how `with` works under the hood rather than treating it as record magic.

questions.q: Why are positional records usually a poor fit for EF Core entity types?
choices: EF Core cannot map any type that lacks a parameterless constructor
Records are value types, so EF Core must box every tracked entity
Value equality clashes with identity tracking, and `with` makes untracked copies
Record properties are private, so EF Core cannot read them to build SQL
questions.why: The change tracker cares about identity: two entity instances with equal values are still different rows, and `with` produces a new instance EF Core is not tracking, so edits silently go nowhere. EF Core can bind constructor parameters, so the constructor is not the problem. Records shine as DTOs and value objects instead.
questions.asked: Shows you choose record versus class on purpose, not because records are the newest thing.

questions.q: A class has `required` properties and a constructor that assigns them. What does marking that constructor `[SetsRequiredMembers]` do?
choices: The compiler checks the constructor body assigns every required member
Callers of that constructor no longer need to set the required members
The required members become read-only once that constructor finishes
Missing required members become a warning instead of an error for callers
questions.why: The attribute tells the compiler to trust that this constructor sets everything, so `new User("a@b.c")` compiles without an initialiser. It is not verified: if the body forgets a member, nothing complains and the property stays null. Use it only on constructors that genuinely assign every required member.
questions.asked: Comes up when mixing `required` DTOs with constructors; knowing it is unchecked is the strong answer.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: It does not compile: only records and tuples deconstruct
questions.why: Deconstruction is pattern-based: any type with an accessible `Deconstruct` method (instance or extension) whose out parameters match the count works. Records simply generate that method for you. The first variable receives the first out parameter.
questions.asked: Shows you know that much of C#'s syntax sugar is pattern-based rather than tied to specific types.

questions.q: What does `Span<byte> buffer = stackalloc byte[256];` give you, and what must you watch?
choices: A pinned heap array that the GC frees at the next collection; avoid pinning
A block rented from ArrayPool; you must return it when you have finished
Memory on the current stack frame; keep its size small and bounded
Stack memory that is moved to the heap if the method awaits anything
questions.why: `stackalloc` reserves memory in the current frame, freed automatically on return with no GC cost, and assigning it to a span needs no `unsafe`. The stack is small (about 1 MB by default), so size it from a constant or fall back to `ArrayPool` above a threshold; a user-controlled size can overflow the stack and kill the process.
questions.asked: Allocation-free parsing code uses this; the bounded-size rule is what shows judgement.

questions.q: A method takes a slice of a buffer, awaits a network write, then takes the next slice. What should its buffer parameter be?
choices: `Span<byte>`, because it is the cheapest possible view over the buffer
`ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, calling `.Span` only between the awaits
`ReadOnlySpan<byte>` marked `scoped`, so it may live across the await
`byte*` pinned with `fixed`, so the GC cannot move it during the await
questions.why: `Memory<T>` is an ordinary struct that can sit on the heap, so it survives an await; you take `.Span` for the synchronous work in between. A span is a ref struct and can never be live across an await, and `scoped` only narrows its lifetime further. That is why async stream APIs such as `Stream.WriteAsync` take `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`.
questions.asked: The Span-versus-Memory split is the follow-up to any Span question.

questions.q: In C# 13 (.NET 9), does this compile?
choices: No: ref struct locals are still banned in every async method
Yes, and the span could also be read safely after the await
Yes: the span is not used after the await, so it is allowed
No: AsSpan allocates on the heap, which async methods forbid
questions.why: C# 13 relaxed the rule: async methods and iterators may declare ref struct locals as long as none is live across an `await` or `yield`. Before C# 13 this was error CS4012. Reading `span` after the await is still an error, because it could not be stored in the heap-allocated state machine.
questions.asked: Tests currency with C# 13 and whether you understand why the old rule existed.

questions.q: What is true of `buf` after `byte[] buf = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1000);`?
choices: Its length is exactly 1000 and every element starts as zero
It lives on the stack and is freed when the method returns
It may still be used safely after you pass it to `Return`
Its length is at least 1000, so you must track the count you use
questions.why: The pool hands out arrays from size buckets, so you may get 1024 or more, and the contents may hold another caller's old data. Track your own length and slice with `buf.AsSpan(0, count)`. After `Return` the array belongs to the pool again, and touching it corrupts someone else's work.
questions.asked: Pooling bugs (reading past the real length, using after return) are the classic follow-up.

questions.q: What does this print (using System.Runtime.InteropServices)?
choices: It throws InvalidOperationException because the list changed
It does not compile: a span cannot view a List's contents
questions.why: `AsSpan` returns a view over the list's current backing array. Adding a fourth item exceeds the capacity of 3, so the list copies into a new, larger array, and the span now points at the abandoned one: the write of 99 is lost. There is no version check on spans, which is why the API lives in `CollectionsMarshal`.
questions.asked: Separates people who know a span is a raw view with no safety net from those who treat it as a collection.

questions.q: What does `using Point = (int X, int Y);` at the top of a file allow in C# 12?
choices: Naming a tuple type so that `Point p = (1, 2);` reads clearly
Declaring a new struct type called Point with X and Y fields
Importing a namespace called Point that exposes X and Y
Creating a record named Point with value equality and ToString
questions.why: C# 12 lets a `using` alias name any type, including tuples, arrays and pointer types. The alias is not a new type: `Point` is exactly `(int X, int Y)`, so any matching tuple converts freely. When you need a distinct type with its own behaviour, declare a record struct instead.
questions.asked: A currency check; the strong answer adds that an alias gives no type safety.

questions.q: Why does this EF Core entity initialise the navigation property with `null!`?
choices: It forces Customer to stay null until the query calls Include
It silences the uninitialised warning because EF Core sets it
It makes EF Core load Customer eagerly on every Order query
It marks the relationship optional in the generated schema
questions.why: Nullable analysis warns that a non-nullable property is never assigned (CS8618), but EF Core fills it when materialising, so `null!` tells the compiler to stop. The type stays non-nullable, which also makes the relationship required. The catch: if you forget `Include`, it really is null at runtime, and the compiler cannot see that.
questions.asked: Every EF Core codebase has this line; interviewers check you know what it hides.

questions.q: A library has `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` and `public void Send(string email)`. Why keep `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(email)`?
choices: Annotations are compile-time only, so callers can still pass null
The compiler strips non-nullable checks unless a guard is present
It is what makes the parameter non-nullable in the compiled IL
Without it, the runtime converts a null argument into an empty string
questions.why: Nullable reference types are warnings and metadata; nothing is enforced at runtime. A caller with nullable disabled, using reflection, or writing `null!` can still pass null. A public API should therefore still guard its inputs, while internal code can rely on the analysis.
questions.asked: Checks you know NRT is static analysis, not a type-system guarantee.

questions.q: What is the difference between `int?` and `string?`?
choices: Each compiles to Nullable<T>, so `typeof(string?)` differs from string
`int?` is the Nullable<int> struct; `string?` only annotates string
`string?` is Nullable<string>; `int?` is only a compiler annotation
Each is a compiler annotation only and changes nothing in the IL
questions.why: For value types `?` produces a real type, `Nullable<int>`, with `HasValue` and `Value`. For reference types it is an annotation the compiler uses for warnings; at runtime `string?` is just `string`. That is why unconstrained generic `T?` needs special rules.
questions.asked: The same symbol meaning two things is a common source of confusion; a clear answer shows solid fundamentals.

questions.q: What does `[MemberNotNull(nameof(_title))]` do here?
choices: It throws at runtime if `_title` is still null when the helper returns
It makes `_title` non-nullable everywhere in the class, not just here
It tells the compiler `_title` is non-null after EnsureTitle is called
It stops the compiler from analysing `_title` inside the helper method
questions.why: Flow attributes describe what a method guarantees. After a call to `EnsureTitle`, the analysis treats `_title` as non-null, so `_title.Length` gives no warning. It is also used on helpers called from constructors. Like every NRT attribute it has no runtime effect.
questions.asked: Shows you can make helper methods cooperate with nullable analysis instead of scattering `!`.

questions.q: What does `order is { Customer.Address.Country: "UK" }` evaluate to when `order.Customer` is null?
choices: It throws a NullReferenceException when it reaches Address
It is true if Country would have been null by default anyway
It fails to compile unless Customer is declared non-nullable
It is false, because property patterns null-check each step
questions.why: An extended property pattern (C# 10) is shorthand for nested patterns, and every property pattern includes a not-null test. So a null order, Customer or Address all make the whole expression false, with no exception. That is why it is safer than `order.Customer.Address.Country == "UK"`.
questions.asked: A tidy way to show you write null-safe checks without chains of `?.`.

questions.q: What happens when you build this and call `Label(Status.Shipped)`?
choices: A compile error, because every switch expression must be exhaustive
It returns null, because no arm matched the value it was given
A compiler warning, then a SwitchExpressionException at runtime
It returns an empty string, the default value for a string result
questions.why: A non-exhaustive switch expression is only warning CS8509; at runtime an unmatched value throws `SwitchExpressionException`. Treat the warning as an error. Even with all three members listed the compiler still warns, because an enum can hold any integer, so add a `_` arm that throws.
questions.asked: Shows you know where the exhaustiveness safety net has holes.

questions.q: What happens with this switch expression?
choices: It compiles; `Size(101)` returns "big" as the more specific arm
Compile error: the second arm can never be reached
It compiles with no diagnostics, and every call returns "other"
It compiles with a warning, and every call returns "other"
questions.why: Arms are tested top to bottom, and the compiler rejects an arm that an earlier one already covers (CS8510). Unlike CSS or route matching, there is no most-specific-wins rule, so the discard goes last. The same check catches overlapping ranges written in the wrong order.
questions.asked: Checks you understand arm ordering rather than assuming specificity rules.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: free
It does not compile: `_` cannot appear inside a tuple pattern
It does not compile: relational patterns do not accept decimal
questions.why: A tuple pattern switches on several values at once, and each position can hold its own pattern, including `_` and relational patterns on decimal constants. A non-member with 30 matches neither of the first two arms, so the discard arm wins. This replaces nested ifs for business rules.
questions.asked: Rule tables like pricing or shipping are a natural place to show modern pattern matching.

questions.q: What does `ch is not 'a' or 'b'` actually test?
choices: That ch is neither 'a' nor 'b'
That ch is exactly the character 'b'
That ch is either 'a' or 'b'
That ch is anything other than 'a'
questions.why: `not` binds more tightly than `or`, so this is `(not 'a') or 'b'`, and 'b' is already covered by `not 'a'`. It is true for every character except 'a'. The intended check is `ch is not ('a' or 'b')`.
questions.asked: A real bug pattern found in code review; knowing the precedence rule shows care with combinators.

questions.q: What does this print?
