choices: "email sent", then "caught"
"caught" only
"email sent" only
"caught", then "email sent"
questions.why: Invoking a multicast delegate calls the handlers one after another on the same thread, and an exception from one stops the rest. The second handler never runs. If handlers must be isolated, loop over `GetInvocationList()` and wrap each call in its own try/catch.
questions.asked: Explains why one faulty subscriber can break unrelated features, a real in-process eventing bug.

questions.q: Why does the second line not stop `Save` from running on each click?
choices: `-=` only works on events that declare explicit add and remove accessors
Each lambda is a separate delegate, so no equal handler exists to remove
Lambda handlers are removed only once the GC collects the button itself
`-=` takes effect on the next raise of the event, not immediately
questions.why: Removal looks for a delegate equal to the one you pass, and two lambdas with the same body are different objects, so `-=` silently does nothing. Keep the delegate in a field (or subscribe a method group) and unsubscribe that same instance. Forgotten subscriptions are a classic leak in long-lived publishers.
questions.asked: Unsubscribe bugs cause leaks and double handlers; this checks you know delegate equality.

questions.q: Why is `Placed?.Invoke(this, e)` the standard way to raise an event?
choices: It runs the handlers on the thread pool instead of the caller's thread
It skips the call when nobody has subscribed, reading the field only once
It catches handler exceptions so one bad handler cannot break the rest
It invokes only the handlers that the declaring class itself subscribed
questions.why: An event with no subscribers is null, so calling it directly throws. `?.` reads the delegate once into a temporary, which also avoids the race where another thread unsubscribes between a null check and the call. Handlers still run synchronously, and exceptions still propagate.
questions.asked: Basic event hygiene; the single-read detail is the bonus point.

questions.q: In C# 10 or later, what is the type of `f` in `var f = (int x) => x * 2;`?
choices: `Expression<Func<int, int>>`, an expression tree
`Func<int, int>`, from the lambda's natural type
It does not compile: a lambda needs a target type
A new compiler-generated delegate type per lambda
questions.why: C# 10 gave lambdas a natural type: when the parameter types are known, `var` infers `Func<>` or `Action<>`. Without the `int` annotation it still fails, as the compiler cannot guess x's type. An expression tree is produced only when the target is explicitly `Expression<...>`.
questions.asked: A currency check that also tests delegates versus expression trees.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: 1, then cleanup
1 only, because finally runs only when the iterator completes
1, 2, then cleanup
cleanup, then 1
questions.why: `foreach` disposes the enumerator when the loop exits, even via break, and disposing an iterator runs any pending `finally` blocks. That is how iterators that open files or readers close them early. If you call `GetEnumerator` by hand and never dispose it, the finally really does never run.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know iterators are state machines with disposal, which matters for data readers.

questions.q: Two users share an email. Which one does `users.DistinctBy(u => u.Email)` (.NET 6) keep?
choices: The last one in source order
An arbitrary one, since it is backed by a hash set
The first one in source order
Neither: every duplicated email is removed entirely
questions.why: `DistinctBy` streams the source and yields an element only the first time its key is seen, so the first occurrence wins and order is preserved. To keep the latest instead, order by date descending first. It replaces the old `GroupBy(...).Select(g => g.First())` idiom.
questions.asked: De-duplicating imports is everyday work; knowing which row survives is the detail that matters.

questions.q: A class's equality uses `Id` and `TenantId`. What is the recommended `GetHashCode` body?
choices: `Id.GetHashCode() + TenantId.GetHashCode()`
`base.GetHashCode()`, so each instance stays unique
`HashCode.Combine(Id, TenantId)`
`$"{Id}{TenantId}".GetHashCode()` on a string
questions.why: `HashCode.Combine` mixes the fields well and allocates nothing. Adding hashes collides more often, and building a string allocates on every call. `base.GetHashCode()` is wrong outright: equal objects must have equal hash codes, or dictionaries and sets lose them.
questions.asked: Implementing equality correctly is a fundamentals check; the Equals/GetHashCode contract is the core of it.

questions.q: A job stores `email.GetHashCode()` in the database to pick a user's shard on later runs. What goes wrong on modern .NET?
choices: GetHashCode copies the string first, so it is slow for long values
The result depends on the server culture, so regions disagree
String hash codes are randomised per process, so values change
Every email gets a unique hash, so the column cannot be indexed
questions.why: Since .NET Core, string hashing is seeded randomly for each process to resist hash-flooding attacks, so the same email hashes differently after a restart. `GetHashCode` is only for in-memory hash tables. Persist a stable hash instead, such as `XxHash64` or SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes.
questions.asked: A real production bug when porting .NET Framework code; it shows you know what GetHashCode is for.

questions.q: You catch an exception, store it, and later rethrow it from a different method. How do you keep its original stack trace?
choices: `throw ex;`, which keeps the trace because it is the same object
`throw;` in the later method, even though it is outside a catch
`throw new Exception("failed", ex)`, which merges both traces
`ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw()` in the later method
questions.why: `ExceptionDispatchInfo` captures the exception with its trace and rethrows it, appending the new location rather than replacing it; `await` uses the same mechanism. `throw ex;` resets the trace, and a bare `throw;` compiles only inside a catch block. Wrapping keeps the original only as an inner exception.
questions.asked: Comes up in retry helpers and background queues; it shows you care about diagnosable failures.

questions.q: What does this pattern achieve?
choices: It logs the exception and swallows it, just like an empty catch
It does not compile, since a filter cannot call a method
It logs the exception, which then propagates as if never caught
It logs only after the stack has unwound into this method
questions.why: Exception filters run before the stack unwinds. Because `Log` returns false, the catch never matches, so the exception carries on up with its full stack intact for crash dumps and debuggers. It is a known idiom for logging at a boundary without handling.
questions.asked: Distinguishes people who know filters run before unwinding from those who treat `when` as a nested if.

questions.q: When is a custom exception type worth creating in an application?
choices: For every method, so stack traces show where each error began
Whenever you throw, since built-in exceptions are for the runtime
When callers need to catch that failure and react differently
Only when deriving from ApplicationException, as guidance says
questions.why: A custom type earns its keep when some caller catches it specifically, for example mapping `OrderNotFoundException` to a 404. Otherwise use built-ins such as `ArgumentException` or `InvalidOperationException`. Derive from `Exception`; the guidance against `ApplicationException` is long-standing.
questions.asked: Shows judgement about exception design rather than creating a type for everything.

questions.q: What does this print (System.Collections.Immutable)?
choices: It throws NotSupportedException from Add
questions.why: Immutable collections never change: `Add` returns a new collection that shares most of its structure with the old one, and `roles` is untouched. Discarding the return value is the usual bug. For read-mostly data, `ImmutableArray<T>` or `FrozenSet<T>` are often cheaper.
questions.asked: Checks you understand the API shape of immutable collections before using them in shared state.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: It throws because the list changed after AsReadOnly
It does not compile: ReadOnlyCollection is not IReadOnlyList
questions.why: `AsReadOnly` returns a `ReadOnlyCollection<T>` wrapper, not a copy: callers cannot modify it, but they see every change the owner makes. If you need a snapshot, return `ToArray()` or an immutable collection. Read-only and immutable are different promises.
questions.asked: The read-only-versus-immutable distinction is a favourite API design question.

questions.q: In .NET 9, what does this print?
choices: It throws InvalidOperationException: collection was modified
questions.why: Since .NET Core 3.0, `Dictionary.Remove` and `Clear` no longer invalidate an active enumerator, so removing during a foreach is allowed. `Add` still throws, and `List<T>` still throws on any change. Old .NET Framework code often builds a separate list of keys to remove for this reason.
questions.asked: A detail that shows you have kept up since .NET Framework, and know which mutations are still unsafe.

questions.q: What does `new List<Order>(10_000)` do for you when you know about 10,000 items are coming?
choices: It avoids repeated grow-and-copy steps as the backing array fills
It pre-fills the list with 10,000 null entries for you to overwrite
It caps the list, so adding a 10,001st item throws an exception
It allocates the items on the stack rather than on the heap
questions.why: The argument is the initial capacity. A list starts small and doubles its backing array whenever it is full, copying each time; presizing skips that. `Count` stays 0 until you add items, so indexing into the list still throws.
questions.asked: A cheap, practical optimisation; the capacity-versus-count distinction is the real check.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: dup a@x, printed twice
It throws ArgumentException on the second a@x
dup a@x
Nothing: Add returns void, so it does not compile
questions.why: `HashSet<T>.Add` returns false when the item is already present instead of throwing, so one call both checks and inserts. Only the second "a@x" is a duplicate. `Dictionary.Add` is the one that throws on a duplicate key; `TryAdd` returns a bool like this.
questions.asked: A small idiom that shows you know the collection APIs rather than writing Contains-then-Add.

questions.q: Why prefer `cache.TryGetValue(key, out var v)` to checking `ContainsKey` and then reading `cache[key]`?
choices: ContainsKey throws when the key is not present
The indexer returns default instead of the stored value
TryGetValue does one hash lookup rather than two
TryGetValue locks the dictionary, so it is thread-safe
questions.why: ContainsKey plus the indexer hashes and searches twice; `TryGetValue` does it once and hands you the value. It is not thread-safe: plain `Dictionary` needs external locking or `ConcurrentDictionary` when written from several threads. The indexer throws on a missing key; ContainsKey never does.
questions.asked: An easy idiom check that code reviewers look for in hot paths.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.code:
int[] xs = [10, 20, 30, 40];
Console.WriteLine($"{xs[^1]} {xs[1..^1].Length}");
questions.why: `^1` means one from the end, so the last element, 40. A range's end is exclusive, so `1..^1` takes indices 1 and 2, giving two elements. On arrays and strings a range copies; on spans it slices without allocating.
questions.asked: A currency check; the exclusive-end rule catches people out.

questions.q: What does this System.Text.Json source generation setup give you?
choices: Validation of incoming JSON against the Order class at runtime
Faster JSON, by switching to Newtonsoft.Json behind the scenes
Serialisation code generated at build time, safe for Native AOT
Automatic camelCase names, which the reflection mode cannot do
questions.why: The generator writes the serialisation logic during the build, so there is no reflection at runtime: faster start-up, and it works with trimming and Native AOT, where reflection-based serialisation breaks. It validates nothing extra, and naming policies work in both modes.
questions.asked: Relevant as Native AOT minimal APIs spread; shows you know why reflection is a problem there.

questions.q: Compared with `new Regex(pattern)` inside a method, what does this (.NET 7+) give you?
questions.code:
[GeneratedRegex(@"^\d{5}$")]
private static partial Regex PostcodeRegex();
choices: A matcher generated as C# at build time, with no runtime parsing
A regex that runs on the GPU, which is faster for long input text
A default one-second timeout applied to every match automatically
A pattern that is checked only in debug builds and removed later
questions.why: The regex source generator emits the matching code at compile time, so there is no parsing or compiling on first use, and it works under Native AOT. It also returns one cached instance. Constructing a `Regex` per call re-parses the pattern every time, which is a common hidden cost.
questions.asked: Shows awareness of modern .NET performance defaults that analysers now suggest.

questions.q: A sealed class owns a `FileStream` and a `SqlConnection`. What does its disposal need?
choices: A finaliser that calls Dispose, in case callers forget to
A plain Dispose() that disposes both; no finaliser at all
The full Dispose(bool) pattern with GC.SuppressFinalize
Nothing: the GC disposes managed fields when the object dies
questions.why: Both fields are managed objects that already have their own finalisers or SafeHandles, so the class only has to forward `Dispose`. Finalisers and `Dispose(bool)` are for types that own raw unmanaged handles or are designed for inheritance. The GC reclaims memory but never calls `Dispose` for you.
questions.asked: Many candidates recite the full pattern; knowing when you do not need it is the mid-level answer.

questions.q: A `Money` value object could convert from `decimal`. Why is an `implicit` conversion a poor choice?
choices: Implicit operators cannot be declared on struct types
Explicit operators run faster because they skip boxing
EF Core value converters cannot see implicit operators
It needs a currency it cannot know, yet would run silently
questions.why: The guideline is that implicit conversions must be lossless and never throw, because they happen without any visible cast. A bare decimal has no currency, so a silent conversion invites bugs such as adding pounds to euros. Use a factory like `Money.Gbp(10m)` or an explicit operator.
questions.asked: Value objects are common in domain code; this checks you design their APIs defensively.

questions.q: For a small `Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)` created in hot loops, why pick `readonly record struct` over `record`?
choices: It avoids a heap allocation per value while keeping value equality
Only structs get value equality; a record class compares references
A record class cannot be made immutable, while a readonly struct can
Structs are always passed by reference, so they are never copied
questions.why: A record struct lives inline (on the stack or inside its container), so creating millions costs no GC work, and `readonly` keeps it immutable with the compiler-generated equality. Record classes also have value equality and are immutable by default; they simply allocate. Keep structs small, since every assignment copies them.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can weigh allocation against copying when choosing a type kind.
